title: University Admissions Handbook 2025/2026
text:
- 118 -ACADEMIC YEAR 2025/2026 UNIVERSITY GRANTS COMMISSION
4.1 Application procedure
i. Applications for university admission will be invited by the UGC by means of notices 
published in the press. Candidates should submit their applications online following the 
instructions given in the Section 5 of the handbook.
 
ii. It will be the responsibility of each applicant to send the printed online application form 
by registered post together with the relevant documents to be received by the UGC 
before the due date. The last date for the receipt of applications for admission will be 
specified in the press notice referred to above. Failure to submit the relevant documents 
and certificates along with the application may result in rejection of the application for 
university admission.
iii. Every candidate who sat the G.C.E. (Advanced Level) Examination as a school candidate 
must have his/ her printed online application form for admission certified by the principal of 
the school from which the candidate presented himself/ herself for the G.C.E. (Advanced 
Level) Examination to obtain the minimum requirements for admission. Every candidate 
who sat the G.C.E. (Advanced Level) Examination, as a private candidate should have 
his/ her printed online application form attested by a Commissioner for Oaths/ Justice 
of Peace.
iv. The successful candidates will be informed of their course of study and the university 
to which they have been selected by the UGC. If the candidate accepts the offer, should 
make the payment of Rs. 50/= as the registration fee to the bank or online in credit of the 
University Grants Commission and register online via the official website of UGC for the 
selected course of study of the university on or before the last date given for registration 
by the UGC.
v. After the online registration, the students should send the duly signed printed form of the 
online registration (Online Payment Receipt) along with evidence of required payment 
if paid to bank (Paying-in-voucher), via registered post to reach the UGC. 
SECTION 4
Application procedure and other important instructions
 Important:
 It is a compulsory requirement to apply for university admission online. 
Important:
Anti-Ragging Declaration made by the student
At the end of the online registration, you are required to download and print in an A4 
paper (both side) the “Anti-Ragging Declaration made by the student”. It is compulsory 
to submit the duly filled and signed declaration to the university at the time of enrollment. 
Please do not send this Declaration to the University Grants Commission through post.

title: University Admissions Handbook 2025/2026
text:
- 119 -ACADEMIC YEAR 2025/2026 UNIVERSITY GRANTS COMMISSION
 4.2 Procedure for filling of vacancies/ method adopted for not getting selected to some 
of the higher preferred courses of study of universities under filling of vacancies 
or to remain in the currently selected course of study and the university without 
getting elevated to any of the higher preferences under filling of vacancies
 4.2.1 Criteria for filling of vacancies 
Vacancies may arise in a particular course of study of a university as a result of non-
registration of students selected under the normal intake. These vacancies are filled 
subject to the provisions made in Section 3.2 of this handbook on the following basis; 
(i) Vacancies arisen in a particular course of study of a particular university (Uni-Code) 
due to non-registration of students selected under the merit quota will be filled by the 
students next in line on an all island merit basis.
(ii) Vacancies arisen in a particular course of study of a particular university (Uni-Code) 
due to non-registration of students selected under the district quota will be filled by 
the students next in line on a district merit basis. Vacancies in a particular district will 
be filled with students from the same district. 
(iii) When an additional number of students have been selected over and above the 
district and merit quota due to clustering of students at the same mark point or any 
other practical reason, such additional number will be deducted from the number of 
vacancies and only the balance will be filled. 
 
(iv) Also in the filling of vacancies, both the course of study and the university to which 
candidate has given preference will be considered together.
 If a particular candidate has not indicated a preference to a course of study of a 
university (Uni-code) for which he/ she could have been selected based on Z-score 
he/ she would not be selected to that course of study of a university for which he/ 
she has not indicated a preference. Instead, he/ she would be considered to the next 
choice of course of study of the university (Uni-Code) preferred by him/ her. 
(v) Vacancies in any course of study will not be filled after the commencement of the 
academic programme of the university concerned without the consent of the Dean of 
the respective Faculty. “Commencement of academic programme” specified above 
does not mean the commencement of an orientation programme including the English 
course.
Very Important:
 4.2.2 For students who wish not to get selected for some of the higher preferred 
courses of study of universities (Uni-Codes) under filling of vacancies or to 
remain in the currently selected course of study and the university without 
getting elevated to any of the higher preferences under filling of vacancies.
(i) When a candidate getting registered to a course of study of a university or a 
higher educational institute (Uni-Code) to which he/ she got selected under the 
normal intake or filling of vacancies on the basis of the results of the G.C.E 
(Advanced Level) Examination held for the year 2025, if he/ she wishes not 
to be considered for some of the courses of study of universities (Uni-Codes) 
in future rounds of filling of vacancies to which he/ she has given higher

preferences than the currently selected course of study of the university (Uni-Code) 
in the application form for university admission or wishes to remain in the course of 
study of the university (Uni-Code) currently selected without getting promoted to 
any of the higher preferred courses of study of the universities under future rounds 
of filling of vacancies, should follow the following steps when getting registered 
online for the course of study of the university (Uni-Code) currently selected.
 1. Click on the “Promotion Declaration” button. 
 2. Then, the list of higher preferred Uni-Codes than the currently selected course 
of study of the university, arranged according to your order of preference will 
be displayed. 
 3. Carefully select the Uni-Codes for which you do not want to be considered 
under future rounds of filling of vacancies for which you have given higher 
preferences than the already selected Uni-Code (put a “ ” mark in relevant

courses of study of universities (Uni-Codes) in future for which you have given 
higher preferences and wish to remain in the already selected course of study 
of university, you may click on the check box in the last column of the header 
row to select all the Uni-Codes in one go. The Uni-Codes selected by you for 
removal will be striked off. 
4. Then, click on the “REMOVE SELECTED HIGHER PREFERENCES” 
button to remove your unwanted Uni-Codes from the database. When you 
click on the “ REMOVE SELECTED HIGHER PREFERENCES” button, 
the window will not get closed, instead your database will be updated. Next, 
click on the Back button to go back to the previous page (The Uni-Codes which 
you have selected as unwanted Uni-Codes for filling of vacancies will also be 
displayed in the Online Payment Receipt generated at the end of the online 
registration process).
5. If you want to re-change the Uni-Codes list which you have selected for removal, 
you can repeat the steps (1) to (4) above.
 
 6. If you fa il to remove the courses of study of universities (Uni-Codes) for 
which you do not want to be considered in future rounds of filling of 
vacancies, you should accept and get registered for the course of study 
of a university to which you would be elevated according to the higher 
preferences indicated in the application form for admission.
(ii) Vacancies are filled in several steps according to the above criteria until the proposed 
intake of a particular course of study of a university is filled.
(iii) According to the example given in the next page, presume that a candidate is selected 
to the course of study in Biological Science at University of Colombo (8th preference) 
based on the cut off marks for university admission. 
 In the filling of vacancies, candidate may be selected to the course of study in 
Radiography at University of Peradeniya (6 th preference) or Physiotherapy in 
University of Colombo (5th preference).

4.3 Procedure to obtain a transfer from one university to another for the same course
 of study
 When vacancies are filled candidates may be selected to a course of study of a university or 
a higher educational institute (Uni-Code) for which they have given a higher preference.
 Therefore, candidates do not need to send a separate request to be selected to the same course 
of study conducted by a different university of higher preference given in the application. 
 Also, please note that mutual transfers are not allowed under any circumstances.
 Courses of study and universities for which the candidates have indicated higher preferences 
are offered based on the vacancies available for those courses of study and universities on 
the basis of Z-score as per the criteria in the Section 4.2 above.

title: University Admissions Handbook 2025/2026
text:
- 122 -ACADEMIC YEAR 2025/2026 UNIVERSITY GRANTS COMMISSION
Candidates who wish to be selected for a course of study and a university for which he/
she has indicated a lower preference should make an appeal as per the instructions given 
in the Section 4.4. 
4.4 Procedure to Make an appeal
After the completion of selection of candidates for admission under the normal intake for 
the academic year 2025/2026, the UGC will appoint an Appeals Committee to investigate 
and report on appeals made by candidates regarding the admission under the normal intake. 
Appeals will be entertained from the following:
(a) Applicants who fall within the declared minimum Z-Score for selection for a particular 
course of study of a university for which the requirements for university admission have 
been fulfilled but not selected, subject to provisions made in Section 3 of this handbook.
(b) Applicants who have been selected for a particular course of study of a university, but 
consider that they qualify to be selected for another course of study of a university indicated 
by them for which the requirements for university admission have been fulfilled, subject 
to provisions made in Section 3 of this handbook.
(c) Applicants who request that their course of study of the university / higher educational 
institute be changed to another course of study of a university/ higher educational institute 
to which they have given a lower preference for which the requirements for admission have 
been fulfilled (In order to consider appeals for a change of course of study of a university/ 
higher educational institute there should be vacancies in the relevant course of study of 
the university/higher educational institute. Students’order of Z-Score will be taken into 
consideration when there are more students who have appealed than vacancies). 
(d) Applicants who failed to apply for a particular course of study of a university / higher 
educational institute for which the requirements for admission have been fulfilled (In 
order to consider appeals under this category there should be vacancies in the relevant 
course of study of the university/ higher educational institute. Students’ order of Z-Score 
will be taken into consideration when there are more students who have appealed than 
vacancies).
 The Appeals Committee will not consider appeals made in respect of the following and 
such appeals will not be acknowledged and payments will not be refunded. 
i. Admission under special provisions
ii. Admission for special subjects under an additional intake
iii. Admission under filling of vacancies 
Those who wish to make an appeal should fill the specimen application mentioned in Annex-
I of the Section 10 of this handbook and send under registered cover to reach the Secre -
tary - Appeals Committee on University Admissions, University Grants Commission, No. 
20, Ward Place, Colombo 07 mentioning the words “ Appeals - University Admissions” on the 
top left hand corner of the envelop or handover to the Public Relations Office at the University 
Grants Commission within three (03) weeks from the date of publishing the Cut-Off-Points 
(COPs). If you handover to the Public Relations Office at the University Grants Commission, 
the acknowledgement receipt issued at the time of handover should be kept with oneself. 
A payment of Rs. 500/= should be made for every appeal. This payment should be made 
to the credit of the UGC Collection Account No. 0002323287 at Torrington Branch of the

Every appeal should be accompanied by the counterfoil of the paying-in-voucher

without this payment. Also, incomplete or appeals with unclear reasons will be rejected.

4.5 Procedure to make a complaint/ objection regarding selection of a particular student 
 for a course of study/ university
 Persons who wish to object to the selection of a particular student for a given course of study 
of a university on the ground that he/she is not qualified for selection, can do so in writing to 
the Deputy Secretary/ University Admissions, University Grants Commission, No 20, Ward 
Place, Colombo 07.
When a complaint is made, the complainant should give as much information as possible about 
the student whose selection is objected to, stating the nature of the objection and wherever 
possible produce documentary evidence in support of the objection.
4.6 Postponement of admission
 (i) If an y cand idate selected for admission to a course of study of a university expects to 
 obtain a postponement of his/ her admission, he/ she may be granted such postponement 
 provided that the university concerned is satisfied with the reasons adduced by the candidate. 
 (ii) In every such case, the student should register at the UGC for the course of study of the 
university/ higher educational institute to which he/ she has been selected in the first instance, 
and an application be made to the Registrar of the respective university indicating the specific 
grounds on which the postponement is sought before the commencement of the academic 
year.
 (iii) The maximum period for which such postponement is given will be one academic year.
 (iv) When a postpo nement is giv en, the candidate will be admitted to the same course of 
 study of the university/ higher educational institute for which he/ she was selected earlier. Any 
 candidate obtaining a postponement of admission will not be eligible to seek admission to
 any other course of study of a university/ higher educational institute on the basis of the
results of a G.C.E. (Advanced Level) Examination held in a later year, after the G.C.E. 
(Advanced Level) Examination held for the year 2025.
Appeals sent through fax or e-mail will not be considered. 
Specimen form for appeals is also available on the UGC web site - www.ugc.ac.lk
If you wish to send more than one appeal, you can use a photocopy of the specimen 
form for appeals.

- 124 -ACADEMIC YEAR 2025/2026 UNIVERSITY GRANTS COMMISSION
4.7 Cancelling university admissions application/ university admission
 If an applicant wishes to cancel their university admissions application/university 
admission, they must notify the University Grants Commission via the Email address 
cancelreq@ugc.ac.lk. After such notification, instructions required to cancel the university 
admissions application/university admission will be provided to the applicant by the 
University Grants Commission via Email.
 If the applicant is selected to a course of study and has already enrolled at the relevant 
university after registering at the University Grants Commission, the candidate must first 
cancel their entrolment at the university and then notify the University Grants Commission in 
the manner mentioned above, along with a copy of the letter issued by the relevant university 
confirming it, in order to cancel their university admission.
 According to the Universities Act No. 16 of 1978 (as amended), the authority to select 
students for university admission is vested in the University Grants Commission, and therefore 
applicants seeking to cancel their university admission must follow the above-mentioned 
procedure and get confirmed the cancellation of their university admission.
4.8 Inquiries on university admission
 All correspondence regarding admission to undergraduate courses should be addressed to;

METHOD OF ONLINE APPLICATION FOR UNIVERSITY ADMISSION
This section explains the method to apply online for courses of study and universities of 
preference. Clear instructions on completing the online application are provided here 
and if you are a candidate who is unable or does not have facilities to apply online, the 
facilities provided in that regard also have been mentioned here. 
Please note that it is compulsory to apply for university admission as well as to get

must compulsorily use the online systems when applying for university admission as 
well as getting registered for the selected course of study of the university. 
UGC team will take the responsibility for the accuracy and the safety of the online 
systems.

STEP 4 - Courses of Study and Universities according to your order of preference
 Please carefully read Section 3.1 of this handbook before filling your order of preference 
for courses and universities. 
 Applicants should clearly understand that in the selection, both the particular course 
of study and the relevant university, for which they have marked a preference will be 
considered together. Candidates will not be considered for the courses of study and 
the universities for which they have not marked a preference, even though they have 
obtained minimum Z-Score marks for the course of study.
 The below given example shows how to fill the Step 4
  Select a course of study from the “Courses” drop down list.

  Then the “University” drop down list will display the universities in which the selected 
course of study is conducted.
  Select a university as per your preference from the list and click “Add” button.
  You should not enter the same course of study with the same university more than one 
instance in your order of preference.
  Once you selected all the preferable courses and universities, you can view all selected 
courses & universities in your order of preference.
  You can change your order of the preference by clicking on the “˅” and “˄” buttons 
which are at the top of this list.
  If you need to remove a course and a university, you can use “x” button to remove from 
the list.
Please note that you can select only the courses of study for which you are eligible 
based on the three subjects offered at the G.C.E. (Advanced Level) Examination.
The example in the next page shows how to prepare the order of preference for courses of study 
& universities.

a few places for special categories of students such as those who have excelled in sports, 
arts and culture, blind and differently abled, personnel of armed forces, teachers and foreign 
students. 
 Only a very few number is admitted on the special grounds specified above. 
 The special categories of candidates who qualify for special admission to universities in Sri 
Lanka are described below.

title: University Admissions Handbook 2025/2026
text:
- 166 -ACADEMIC YEAR 2025/2026 UNIVERSITY GRANTS COMMISSION
 It is important to note th at, only candidate s who satisfy the minimum requirements for 
university admission (set out in Section 1.2 of this Handbook) and the appropriate subject 
pre-requisites (set out in Section 2.2 of this handbook) for the relevant course of study will 
be considered under this special provision. 
 Ap plicants are required to submit medical certificates acceptable to the UGC in proof of their 
physical disability in any occasion as requested by UGC. For the purpose of this section, 
physical disability shall mean a permanent physical impairment which has affected normal 
life.
 
6.2 Students who have Excelled in Extra Curricular Activities
 Up to 0.5% of the places from the proposed intake in each course of study other than courses
 offered by the University of the Visual and Performing Arts have been reserved for candidates who
 have obtained 1st, 2nd or 3rd places at national level and / or achievements at international levels in
 such fields as sports, cultural activities (E.g. dancing, painting, music and literature), scouting and
 cadetting, social work and other extra curricular activities between 01.01.2023 to 31.12.2025 but
 have failed to gain admission under the normal intake because of the shortfall of a few Z - scores.
In the case of the University of the Visual and Performing Arts up to 4% of the places from 
the proposed intake in each course of study have been reserved for the admission of students 
under this category.
In order to be eligible for admission under this provision, candidates should have satisfied 
the minimum requirements specified in Section 1.2 and subject pre-requisites for admission 
to a particular course of study specified in Section 2.2 of this handbook.
Candidates who are within a Z – score of 0.2000 of the cut-off-point applicable to the admission 
district of the candidate in the relevant course of study will only be considered for admission 
and should be summoned for an interview.
Candidates who are eligible under this scheme are required to produce documentary evidence 
with regard to their achievements at national/ international level when they are summoned 
for an interview at the UGC Secretariat.
Marks will be awarded for their achievements at the interview in accordance with a marking 
scheme approved by the UGC. Final selection will be made in order of the marks that applicants 
obtain at this evaluation, depending on the places available under this special provision. 
For selection of candidates, marks scored at this evaluation will not be added to the Z-score 
marks obtained by applicants at the G.C.E. (Advanced Level) Examination. 
 Applications for admission under the category of blind and differently abled candidates 
specified above should be made in the prescribed form appearing at the Annex-III of 
this handbook. 
 The duly perfected application forms of the differently abled candidates attached with 
the certified copies of medical reports should be sent along with the applications for 
university admission to reach the Deputy Secretary/ University Admissions, University 
Grants Commission, No. 20, Ward Place, Colombo 07 on or before the closing date for 
calling applications for university admission as specified in the press notice. 
 Incomplete applications and applications received after the due date will be rejected. No 
press notices will be published calling for applications under this provision separately.

title: University Admissions Handbook 2025/2026
text:
- 167 -ACADEMIC YEAR 2025/2026 UNIVERSITY GRANTS COMMISSION
6.3 Candidates with Exceptional Abilities / Skills in Sports
 A small number of places over and above the proposed intake for the course of study in
 Sports Science & Management conducted by the Sabaragamuwa University of Sri Lanka and
University of Sri Jayewardenepura, for the course of study in Sports Science conducted by 
the University of Kelaniya and for the course of study in Physical Education conducted by 
the Sabaragamuwa University of Sri Lanka and University of Jaffna will be allocated to the 
candidates who have excelled in Sports. 
The requirements to be fulfilled for this special admission are as follows.
 • Winning Medals or participation in Olympic Games. 
• Winning at least Gold, Silver or Bronze Medals in Commonwealth Games, Asian 
Games or SAARC Games.
 • Member of a national team representing Sri Lanka at Commonwealth Games, Asian 
Games, SAARC Games or in a recognized World Cup in a sport such as Cricket, 
Football, Rugby, V olleyball, Netball or any other sport as decided by the University 
Grants Commission.
 The candidates selected for admission under this special category should follow a 
suitable foundation course organized by the Open University of Sri Lanka before 
commencing of the academic programme.
 A press notice will be published calling for applications under this special provision 
separately.
Applications for admission under the category of students who have excelled in extra 
curricular activities specified above should be made in the prescribed form appearing at 
the Annex-II of this handbook, by indicating the courses of study to which you wish to be 
considered for admission according to your order of preference. Please refer Annex (a) for 
the mapping table of courses of study. Applications which do not indicate the course codes 
given in Annex (a) will be rejected without any notice.
The duly perfected application form given in Annex - II with the signature and the official 
frank of the principal of your school and the certified copies of the certificates relevant to 
your achievements during the period from 01.01.2023 to 31.12.2025, should be sent along with 
the printed application for university admission to reach the Deputy Secretary/ University 
Admissions,University Grants Commission, No.20, Ward Place, Colombo 07 on or before 
the closing date for applications as specified in the press notice. 
If the student is unable to attend the interview for the above provision, the parent or guardian 
of that student could attend the interview on behalf of the student in the relevant day with 
a letter from the student, due to a reason acceptable by the University Grants Commission. 
However, permission to the same should be obtained from the University Grants Commission 
in advance.
 Incomplete applications and applications received after the due date will be rejected. 
 No press notices will be published calling for applications under this provision separately.

title: University Admissions Handbook 2025/2026
text:
- 168 -ACADEMIC YEAR 2025/2026 UNIVERSITY GRANTS COMMISSION
 6.4 Enlisted Personnel of Armed Forces, Police Service & Special Task Force
Following places are reserved for the courses of study in Engineering, Medicine and Dental 
Surgery under this special provision;
(i). Up to 0.5% of the places from the proposed intake are reserved in the courses of study 
in Medicine and Engineering for personnel enlisted in the Armed Forces, and the Police 
Service and the Special Task Force serving in operational areas. 
(ii). Up to 0.5% of the places from the proposed intake are reserved in the course of study in 
Dental Surgery for the Police Service and the Special Task Force serving in operational 
areas. 
 And,
 Up to 5 students over and above the proposed intake are reserved in the course of study 
in Dental Surgery for the personnel enlisted in the Armed Forces according to the Cabinet 
Paper No: 21/2026/303/156 dated 14.12.2021. 
Candidates who wish to apply under this provision s hould have satisfied the minimum 
requirements for admission specified in the Section 1.2 and subject pre-requisites for admission 
to the above mentioned courses of study specified in Section 2.2 of this handbook and should 
have got enlisted at the time of sending the application to the Secretary of the Ministry of 
Defence, through the Commander of the Service concerned. Out of the applications forwarded 
by the Secretary of the Ministry of Defence, the eligible candidates will be selected based on 
the average Z-Score obtained by the candidates at the G.C.E. (Advanced Level) Examination. 
Candidates should not apply directly to the UGC for this intake and applications are only 
accepted by the Secretary of the Ministry of Defence.
 6.5 Sri Lankans who have Studied Abroad and Foreign Students
(i) Up to 0.5% of the places from the proposed intake in each course of study have been 
allocated to foreign students and Sri Lankan students who have obtained qualifications 
abroad. Accordingly, candidates with results at a foreign examination held outside 
Sri Lanka deemed equivalent to G.C.E. (Advanced Level) Examination of Sri Lanka 
are eligible to apply for admission to universities in Sri Lanka.
Selections are based on the following order of priority:
(a) Children of Sri Lankan diplomatic personnel who are/have been stationed in other 
countries provided they have received education abroad for at least three academic 
years in the six-year period immediately preceding the qualifying examination.
(b) Children of foreign diplomatic personnel working in Sri Lanka.
(c) Students from SAARC countries.
(d) Sri Lankan students not covered under (a) above provided that they have obtained 
qualifications for university admission after studying abroad for not less than three 
academic years immediately preceding the qualifying examination.
(e) Other foreign students not covered under (b) or (c) above.
The parents of the Sri Lankan candidates of categories (a) & (d) above should also have 
worked in the same country during the three academic year period considered for admission 
under this provision.

title: University Admissions Handbook 2025/2026
text:
- 169 -ACADEMIC YEAR 2025/2026 UNIVERSITY GRANTS COMMISSION
All selected candidates will be admitted on fee levying basis except for the candidates 
under category (a) above.
(ii) In addition, up to 4.5% of the places over and above the proposed intake in each course 
of study will be allocated on fee levying basis to foreign students and Sri Lankan 
students who have obtained qualifications abroad.
The parents of the Sri Lankan candidates considered under this 4.5% provision should also 
have worked in the same country during the three academic year period considered for 
admission under this provision.
All prospective candidates should download the relevant applications from the official website 
of the UGC (www.ugc.ac.lk).
6.6 Admission of Teachers
 The University Grants Commission may admit a limited number of teachers to courses of 
study in Arts, Biological Science, Physical Science and Applied Sciences each year belonging 
to the following categories:
(a) Teachers who have passed the General Arts Qualifying (External) Examination/ 
First Examination in Bachelor of Arts (External) in or after 2021 having offered 
English as one of the subjects for a course of study in Arts.
(b) Teachers who have passed the First Examination in Bachelor of Science (External) 
Degree Programme in or after 2021 for courses of study in Biological Science, 
Physical Science or Applied Sciences.
In order to be eligible for admission, a teacher belonging to either of the above categories 
should:
(1) Have completed at least 5 years of service as a teacher from the date of the first 
appointment.
(2) Not be enrolled as a student in any Teacher Training College/ College of Education 
at the time of selection and
(3) In the case of Biological Science or Physical Science or Applied Sciences a candidate 
should have obtained passes in the relevant subjects at the G.C.E. (Advanced Level) 
Examination or the First Examination in Bachelor of Science (External) Degree 
Programme as a pre-requisite to be selected for a course of study available in a 
University.
The Secretary of the Ministry of Education, Higher Education and V ocational Education 
through a Government Gazette Notification will entertain applications for admission of 
teachers under this special provision. Selections will be made by the UGC based on the 
performance (Aggregate and/ or marks obtained for the relevant subjects) of candidates at 
the General Arts Qualifying (External) Examination/ First Examination in Bachelor of Arts 
(External) or the First Examination in Bachelor of Science (External) Degree Programme 
& based on the performance at the interview held by the UGC. Candidates should not send 
applications directly to the UGC.

title: University Admissions Handbook 2025/2026
text:
- 170 -ACADEMIC YEAR 2025/2026 UNIVERSITY GRANTS COMMISSION
6.7 Additional Intake
For some subjects in the course of study in Arts, an adequate number of students may not be 
selected on the basis of the admissions policy specified in Section 1.1 in this handbook. As a 
result, some Faculties and Departments could be in a position to admit a larger number than 
the number selected under the normal admission criteria. 
In such circumstances, the UGC m ay, at the request of the Universities concerned, decide 
to admit a limited number of additional students for the selected subject areas. This is ‘an 
additional intake’ aimed at making optimal use of the human and physical resources available 
at Universities, as well as meeting skilled manpower needs of the society.
Since candidates are selected out of those who have already applied for the normal intake, 
no separate application need to be made for selection under the Additional Intake. 
Students u nder this provision will be selected based on the All Island Merit. However, 
for Language subjects, Religion and Civilization subjects and Aesthetic Studies subjects, 
candidate should have necessarily obtained at least a “C” Grade for the subject (in the case 
of English Language minimum requirement is a “S” Grade) for which he/ she would be 
considered. 
Successful candidates shoul d study this subject area throughout the duration of his/ her 
university education. If the candidate intends to obtain a specialized degree he/ she should 
select the same subject to which he/ she was selected under this special provision.
Teachers selected for admission under this special provision should be prepared to 
follow the courses of study which are offered to them.
All selected candidates will be admitted to the first year of study.

title: How to Support a Jobseeker?
text:
III 
 X Preface
In recent years, successive crises (financial, climatic, health, geopolitical and so on) have hit the 
global economy and had a powerful impact on the labour market, increasing inequalities. The most 
disadvantaged populations (young people, women, people with disabilities, the elderly, migrants, 
refugees and so on) have been the hardest hit. For many, the loss of jobs and income due to the crisis 
directly threatens their daily survival. Ensuring that these disadvantaged groups are not left behind 
during the crisis and when the economy recovers is essential to advancing social justice, which is a 
necessary foundation for the proper functioning of our societies and for sustainable peace.
For the ILO and its constituents, advancing social justice means fair and equal treatment for all; in 
particular, equal opportunities in accessing the benefits of economic growth, regardless of origin, 
age, gender, creed, disability and social and economic status, by promoting decent work, respect for 
fundamental principles and rights at work, fair wages and social protection for all.
Active labour market policies (ALMPs) are essential to promoting equal opportunities by facilitating 
access to employment for the most disadvantaged. Employment services form an integral part of ALMPs 
as an implementation mechanism. In addition, public and private employment services are essential to 
supporting individuals in managing career transitions in a constantly changing market, through career 
guidance, training and job information. At the same time, they contribute to ensuring that the economy 
functions better. Employment services are an important labour market institution that contributes to the 
empowerment of people, connects jobseekers with employers and plays a key role in the functioning of 
labour markets.
However, we frequently find that the tools and training available to “employment counsellors” in 
employment services need to be adapted to meet the new challenges of the labour market, linked to 
the future of work, multiple crises and geopolitical tensions. The ILO has therefore embarked on an 
initiative aimed at providing a collection of practical guides entitled “Building my future at work” to 
support “Employment Counsellors”. These publications are available free of charge in several languages 
on the ILO website.
If you are an “employment counsellor”, this handbook is aimed directly at you, especially if you have been 
recently recruited. It aims to provide valuable tools for your work in employment services. I am convinced 
that this publication will be useful in your work and will strengthen your role within the institution of the 
employment service.
Ms Sukti DASGUPTA
Head of the Employment, Labour Market and Youth branch.
International Labour Organization – Geneva

title: How to Support a Jobseeker?
text:
X Introduction
The world of work is constantly changing. The economy is forced to adapt to environmental, technological, 
demographic, political and social challenges. New professions are being created, some are disappearing, 
all are being transformed. In order to successfully manage transitions in their careers, at different points 
in their working lives, individuals need advice and even coaching. Employment services play a major role 
in facilitating these transitions and in intermediating between job supply and demand. If you have just 
taken up a job as an employment counsellor, be proud of the job you are going to do. Your action will 
have an impact on the professional and personal futures of the many individuals whom you will advise 
and support.
This manual is yours. More generally, it is aimed at all those involved in professional integration, whether 
in a public employment service, an association, a private employment agency or a training organization. 
In the vast majority of countries there are no training courses to prepare for the profession of professional 
integration or employment counsellor. Generally, candidates for these positions come from a wide variety 
of backgrounds and discover the job in situ. In the best of cases, they will benefit from a post-recruitment 
training cycle to accompany them in their new position. But often they will learn the profession without 
traditional training, just by observing the practices of their more experienced colleagues. 
The aim of this handbook is to provide you with the elements that will help you to understand and 
practise the job of an employment counsellor. Designed in three complementary parts, it provides you 
with a conceptual framework, methodological elements and environmental elements. It is designed to be 
used in conjunction with the two practical guides 
already published by the ILO (free access on the 
website): 
 X How to choose my future profession? 
 X How to organize my job search? 
Of course this manual is not exhaustive. It provides 
you with the basis for your new job, it provides 
the knowledge and skills needed to do it, but it 
does not replace a training course, which every 
employment counsellor should have. 
Finally, like the two practical guides, this manual is designed to be used globally, without reference to 
any one country or continent. Everyone will have to adapt it to the context and realities of their country 
and professional environment. 
We hope that it will be useful to you as you discover your new profession as a counsellor and build the 
foundations of your professional practice. 
Mr François DUMORA

Employment services specialist

title: How to Support a Jobseeker?
text:
X Work: a fundamental right
On 10 December 1948, the General Assembly of the United Nations adopted the Universal Declaration 
of Human Rights, Article 23 of which states that: 
 X “Everyone has the right to work, to free choice of employment, to just and favourable conditions of 
work and to protection against unemployment. 
 X Everyone, without any discrimination, has the right to equal pay for equal work. 
 X Everyone who works has the right to just and favourable remuneration ensuring for himself and his 
family an existence worthy of human dignity, and supplemented, if necessary, by other means of 
social protection.” 
Work is therefore a fundamental right that should enable every human being to live in dignity. The 
International Labour Organization, created in 1919, is responsible for defending this right. Bringing 
together representatives of governments, employers and workers from its 187 member states, it 
negotiates and sets international labour standards, develops policies and designs programmes to 
advance social justice and promote decent work for all women and men around the world. 
 X Realities of labour around the world
There is much progress still to be made. 
Today, around the world (1)
 X 160 million children – 63 million girls and 97 million boys – are engaged in child labour. This 
equates to more than 1 in 10 children on our planet. Nearly half of them perform work that directly 
endangers their health, safety and moral development.
 X 40.3 million people are victims of modern slavery, including 24.9 million in forced labour and 15.4 
million in forced marriage. 1 in 4 victims of modern slavery is a child.
 X On average, women are paid 23 per cent less than their male counterparts. Hundreds of millions 
of people suffer discrimination at work because of their skin colour, ethnic or social origin, religion 
or political opinion, age, gender, sexual identity or orientation, disability or because they are HIV-
positive.
In addition to these most striking situations, the global labour market is characterized above all by a great 
deal of informality, in other words jobs are worked without declaration to the competent authorities, 
without any legal or regulatory framework and without social protection. In many countries in the South, 
informality can account for up to 90 per cent of economic activity. Formal employment is the exception 
and precariousness the norm. Thus, having a job does not guarantee any escape from poverty and about 
half of the world's population lives on the equivalent of 2 dollars a day. 
In adopting its Sustainable Development Agenda in 2015, the United Nations identified 17 major goals. 
The eighth aims to promote sustainable and shared economic growth, employment and decent work for 
all. This target constitutes the guideline for the work of the ILO for the decade.
2

situations. The most affected are always the most vulnerable populations: women, young people, people

with disabilities, refugees and migrants. According to the ILO Observatory, more than 144 million jobs 
were lost globally as a result of the COVID-19 crisis between 2019 and 2021 (2).
But the climate crisis is probably the greatest challenge of our time. Because of the environmental 
degradation it causes, climate change poses a considerable risk to the economy by reducing productivity 
and destroying jobs. 
Droughts, heat waves, heavy rainstorms, tropical cyclones, rising sea levels, increasing temperatures and 
changes in rainfall patterns all displace workers, disrupt business activities, damage business equipment 
and infrastructure and negatively impact productivity, the labour market and employment. Moreover, as 
in all crises, the effects disproportionately impact upon the most vulnerable, especially women. 
While the situation may appear very bleak, it is all the more important to be prepared for it, not least 
because the fight against climate change can also create many jobs. According to a 2019 ILO report (3), 
replacing fossil fuels with renewable energy and promoting a circular economy, which involves using 
resources in a sustainable and recyclable way, would create more than 103 million new jobs worldwide. 
 X New economies and accelerated change in 
professions 
The main characteristic of the future of work is an intense acceleration in the evolution of professions, 
which will mainly be linked to technological innovations. All sectors and almost all professions are 
impacted by the possibilities offered by digital technology. Many professions are transforming, others 
are disappearing and new ones are being created.

title: How to Support a Jobseeker?
text:
At the heart of the evolution of professions, we can distinguish the growing importance of five economic 
sectors that will be of major importance over the coming decades: 
 9 The digital economy (platinum) : this covers Information and Communication Technologies 
(ICT), including the computing, electronics and telecommunications sectors, as well as all uses 
generated by the Internet, applications and social networks. 
 9 The green economy : this includes activities that produce goods or services for environmental 
protection or sustainable management of natural resources, as well as traditional activities that 
transform their practices for better environmental quality.
 9 The blue economy : this consists in the sustainable use of ocean resources for economic 
growth, improved incomes and jobs and healthy ocean ecosystems: seafood, transport, tourism, 
energy, shipbuilding and so on.
 9 The care economy (purple) : boosted by global demographics, the need for childminders 
and carers for the elderly is increasing worldwide, generating a large number of jobs over the 
coming years.
 9 The creative economy (orange) : the set of activities consisting in transforming ideas into 
cultural goods and services. The multiplication of communication, leisure and cultural exchange 
media gives ideas and intellectual production unprecedented economic weight 
Employment professionals need to be aware of this context in order to support workers and jobseekers 
in these new realities. 
The days of “a job for life in the same company” no longer exist. These days, it is estimated that each 
employee will have to change job and/or profession at least five times during their career. This figure 
tends to increase regularly. Each employee must therefore keep abreast of the latest developments 
in their sector of activity and profession. They must continuously update their skills so as not to be 
overtaken by technological developments and to be able to bounce back to deal with unforeseen 
circumstances. In general, they must remain alert to opportunities that will be the basis for transferring 
their skills to other positions and other professions. Workers must be the pilots of their professional lives 
and not mere passengers. 
51. The future of work

title: How to Support a Jobseeker?
text:
During the “30 glorious years”, as they are known in France (1945 to 1975), when many countries’ economies 
were booming and employment was plentiful, the situation of the unemployed was often looked upon 
with disdain. It could be said that the unemployed were considered either unlucky and unresourceful or 
lazy and content to live off wider society. Then came the economic crises and mass unemployment set in, 
almost as a matter of course. 
Today, even when the economy is improving, no one is immune to job loss. As explained earlier, the labour 
market is so fluid, and occupations change so quickly, that few individuals do not experience one or more 
periods of unemployment during their career. If it is anticipated, this transition situation can be experienced 
as a break, a stage that can be used to give a new direction to one’s career, to move on to another sector, 
or even another profession, and to develop new skills. However, job loss is often not anticipated by the 
individual. It is often experienced as a trauma. 
 X Cycle of reactions to job loss
For all of us, having a job is first and foremost a source of income that should enable us to meet the 
unavoidable expenses of daily life (food, housing, children’s education, health and so on). In addition 
to meeting these primary needs, work also contributes to personal development and fulfilment. Work 
provides a social status and an identity. It is therefore an important element of psychological well-being. 
This is why the announcement of redundancy and the arrival of unemployment can be very difficult for any 
individual: fears for one's finances, anxieties about the uncertainty of finding a job quickly, loss of identity 
and so on. 
The newly unemployed person will go through intense emotional phases before being able to “mourn” the 
lost job, move on and bounce back. The work of the American-Swiss psychiatrist Elisabeth Kübler-Ross is 
reference literature on this subject. She identifies the stages of the grieving process in the loss of a loved 
one, which are transposed to the loss of a job and more generally to any situation of change.
Negative, past-oriented attitude
Constructive, future-oriented attitude
Grieving process or stages of change – inspired by Elisabeth Kübler-Ross
Shock
Denial
Anger
Sadness/depression
Acceptance
Experimentation
Decision Serenity/confidence
Fear
8
How to support a jobseeker?

title: How to Support a Jobseeker?
text:
It is assumed that each individual necessarily goes through the various stages of this process. The difference 
between individuals is the time spent on each stage. For some it may be a few minutes, for others several 
days, weeks or months. Some people remain permanently stuck in the denial, anger or sadness stage, thus 
sinking into a depression phase.
1. The shock: the individual experiences announcement of the dismissal as something brutal. They do 
not understand what is happening to them. They are in shock.
2. Denial: they are in negation. They do not accept the reality of the dismissal. A great sense of injustice 
overwhelms them. “It’s not possible” – “Why me?”
3. Anger : they let their anger out, and sometimes look for people to blame.
4. Fear: they fear for their future; fear that they will not be able to find another job; fear that they will 
not be able to cover their expenses; and so on.
5. Depression/sadness: they feel powerless and finally give up and/or complain. This stage is special 
because it closes the downward phase of the curve. It is at this point that the individual grasps the 
inescapable nature of the change: either they consent to it and accept the impact on their daily life, 
or they remain locked into their frustration.
6. Acceptance: at the beginning of the upward phase, they begin to change their point of view. Maybe 
the change isn’t such a bad thing?. 
7. Experimentation: through experimentation, they identify the opportunities and benefits of the 
new situation. They can take advantage of this to bounce back.
8. The decision : this is it, they are taking a new look at their job loss. They have come to terms with 
their past and are now looking to the future. This is the time to take stock of your expectations and 
desires in relation to work. “Do I continue in this way? Should I do something else?” And so on.
9. Serenity and confidence: the change has finally been assimilated. The individual has achieved 
serenity and confidence regarding their new situation. They are excited about their new projects. 
It is essential for employment professionals to be fully aware of this grieving process in relation to job loss, 
in order to take it into consideration when welcoming a new jobseeker. Depending on the phase in which 
they find themself, the individual will be more or less available, psychologically, to invest in the stages of 
their return to employment. 
92. Individuals and unemployment

title: How to Support a Jobseeker?
text:
X Vulnerable groups
Although article 1 of the Declaration of Human Rights states that “All human beings are born free and equal 
in dignity and rights”, the facts show that this equality does not extend to the labour market, because it is a 
market and it works according to the laws of supply and demand. Thus, the most qualified and experienced, 
as well as the most resourceful and influential and so on, have a competitive advantage. In this race for 
jobs, those who remain without a decent job solution are often the same: young people without experience, 
women, senior citizens, people with disabilities, migrants and refugees, ethnic minorities, LGBT people 
and so on.
The role of a public employment service is to promote equity and inclusion in the labour market. As a public 
service, it will therefore pay special attention to these vulnerable groups and implement active policies to 
guide them and promote their access to employment.

difficulty entering the labour 
market because of a combination 
of obstacles, often stemming from social organization: less access to education, the burden of 
bringing up children and running the household, and limited access to certain occupations. Although 
the employment situation of women has improved dramatically over the past 50 years, gaps still 
remain. Gender equality in access to work must be a central pillar of employment policies and all 
discrimination must be combated; this begins with the assertion that professions have no gender. All 
jobs must be equally accessible to women and men!

X Seniors : In the world of work, the term “senior” is used 
in two ways:

profession, mainly due to several years of professional

 Northern countries are the most affected by the ageing of populations and the phenomenon of 
underemployment of older people. They are trying to develop incentive policies to keep them 
employed until retirement age. 
 X Persons with disabilities : According to ILO Convention No. 159, adopted in 1983, “the term 
disabled person means an individual whose prospects of securing, retaining and advancing in 
suitable employment are substantially reduced as a result of a duly recognised physical or mental 
impairment.” This same convention, already ratified by 85 countries around the world, encourages 
policies on : 
 X The vocational rehabilitation of people with disabilities.
 X Positive measures aimed at equal opportunities and the promotion of employment 
opportunities for people with disabilities in the open labour market.
In practice, State policies to promote access to employment for people with disabilities are mainly based 
on three strategies : 
 X Obliging companies and administrations to have a minimum percentage of persons with 
disabilities in their workforce.
 X Implementing incentives to hire or keep persons with disabilities in employment: adaptation of 
workstations, financial aid and so on.
 X Creating and subsidizing specific work structures to accommodate, in suitable conditions, 
persons whose disability is too severe to be considered for a job in a traditional company. 
 X Migrants and refugees : Human history is made up of migrations. Famine and insecurity, often 
caused by wars or climatic disasters, have always been the main reasons for people to flee to 
territories considered more favourable. The phenomenon continues in our time and is likely to 
increase as a result of global climate change. Although we are all descendants of migrants, the 
reception and integration of these populations into the society and economy of the country of arrival 
is often problematic. Depending on the legislation, they are not always allowed to work. Employment 
services have a role to play in developing humanistic policies to integrate these populations into 
decent work.

Labour market integration is a process that permits an individual to “find their place” in the labour market; 
in other words, to find a professional activity corresponding to their ambitions and skills, for a period of 
time in line with their project. 
According to Claude TROTTIER, Louise LAFORCE and Renée CLOUTIER (5), the three criteria that characterize 
successful professional integration are: stability in the job found, the training/job match and the 
construction of a professional identity. This third point should be stressed. Indeed, professional integration 
appears to be a socialization process. It would allow a young person to truly move into adulthood and find a 
certain recognition by their peers through identification with a profession and a professional environment. 
One of the challenges of professional integration would therefore be to enable integration into society.
As for the stability criterion, which is often understood as the signing of a long-term employment contract, 
it has long been a prerequisite for successful integration. This is probably less the case today, as we know 
that the labour market is changing and that a professional life is made up of many stages. In addition, many 
young people no longer wish to be locked into a permanent contract. They prefer to multiply the number of 
fixed-term contracts and life experiences. Generations Y and Z have always understood, since birth, that the 
world of work only promises them unemployment and hardship; the prospect of a permanent contract is 
therefore not their ideal. Without confidence in the future, many young people prefer to live in the moment, 
both in their private lives and at work, and prefer to 'zap' from contract to contract. They are nonetheless 
professionally integrated, if this situation corresponds to a non-constrained choice. 
 X Employment services
Depending on the country and the context, the “galaxy” of organizations involved in professional integration 
support may vary but is generally vast (see chapter 11) and made up of entities that are either generalists or 
specialized in a certain sector of society or of activity. In most cases, the Public Employment Service (PES) 
is the central pillar.
The centrality of the PES is given by ILO Convention No. 88 (6). Adopted in 1948 and ratified by 92 countries, 
it very precisely defines the obligations of a government to deploy a free, local public employment service,

title: How to Support a Jobseeker?
text:
According to UNESCO (7), the practice of career guidance is based on the following principles: 
1. Human beings have the capacity and opportunity to make choices concerning their careers. The 
range of options depends in part on individuals’ social, economic and cultural situation. 
2. These options and choices should be open to all, regardless of gender, socioeconomic class, 
religion, disability, sexual orientation, age or cultural background. 
3. Career options are open to individuals throughout their lives. 
4. Over the course of their lives, human beings typically take on a wide range of roles in the world of 
work, which may or may not be remunerated. 
5. Counsellors help individuals to study, pursue and achieve their career goals. 
6. There are essentially four elements to career guidance:
• Helping individuals to become more aware of their interests, values and abilities, as well as 
their own personality. 
• Providing students with access to resources so that they can be better informed about trades 
and professions. 
• Involving students in the decision-making process so that they can choose a career that is well 
suited to their own areas of interest, values, abilities and personality. 
• Helping individuals to manage their careers well (including managing transitions between 
stages and balancing their various social roles) and to become lifelong learners by enhancing 
their professional development throughout their lives. 
7. The reasons why individuals enter certain occupations vary according to the importance that 
they attach either to personal preferences and areas of interest or to external influences, such as 
labour market trends or parental expectations. 
8. Choosing a career is not a single decision in a person’s life but rather an ongoing process that can 
take place at any age. 
9. All professions are useful and contribute to the success and well-being of a society.
Each individual should be free to choose an occupation corresponding to their personality, without 
restriction or discrimination. It is essential to understand that career guidance is not just for school leavers. 
Working lives generally span more than 40 years. Each individual will therefore have to make choices 
along the way, manage transitions and train and orient themselves throughout their lives. Knowing how 
to orientate oneself is a skill that everyone must acquire in order to mitigate the impacts of life’s vagaries. 
In the areas of career guidance, the role of the employment services is. 
 X To provide information on professions, trends and realities in the labour market
 X To provide advice and support to individuals whenever necessary
 X To help individuals acquire the competence to orientate themselves autonomously in order to best 
manage the transitions that they will face during their career.

X Focus on the skills-based approach
The acceleration of changes in the labour 
market is rapidly transforming professions. 
Education and vocational training systems 
are often not responsive enough to adapt 
curricula and syllabuses. The diploma thus 
loses its relevance and importance in favour 
of acquired and practised skills. “The skills-
based approach” means going beyond 
diplomas to focus on skills and abilities to 
act in a professional situation.
A survey of companies in France showed 
that 57 per cent of recruiters look primarily 
at behavioural skills in the selection phase, 
before technical skills. 
 X Focus on the labour market 
Is work a commodity like any other? The use of the expression “labour market” could indeed lead one 
to believe that the price of an hour of work should be determined, like the price of a ton of wheat, 
according to the laws of the market, by searching for a balance between the supply of labour (offered by 
workers) and the demand for labour (expressed by employers). This is the thesis defended by theorists 
of neoclassical economics, which emerged at the end of the nineteenth century. They advocate pure 
and perfect competition that would eliminate unemployment and achieve full employment. For the 
neoclassicals (Pareto, Marshall, Friedman and others), the labour market should self-regulate and there 
should be total wage flexibility. They therefore denounce any barriers to this market, such as regulations 
concerning weekly hours or dismissals, the setting of a minimum wage, or the introduction of any social 
benefits that might encourage voluntary unemployment. 
But workers are not tons of grain. They are human beings with a right to decent work. When neoclassical 
theory is applied, workers can end up being obliged to accept a price per hour and working conditions 
that do not permit them to live decently. All the more so as there is an asymmetry in the negotiation 
between employers and employees (8). Alone, the employee is often at a disadvantage in negotiations. 
Their often precarious situation does not usually allow them to negotiate their skills at a fair price. Their 
precariousness forces them to accept lesser conditions. Regulation is necessary and must take the form 
of State intervention. This is supported by the theories developed by John Maynard Keynes, notably in 
his “General Theory of Employment, Interest and Money”. 
In 1919, at the end of the First World War and on the occasion of the Treaty of Versailles, the International 
Labour Organization was created on the basis of the idea that there can be no lasting and universal 
peace without social justice. Much of the International Labour Organization’s work over the past 100

years has consisted in negotiating international labour law rules to regulate the market, protect workers 
and promote decent work. A total of 190 international conventions have been approved by tripartite 
representatives of governments, employers and workers. They prohibit forced labour, fight against child 
labour and discrimination, and advocate the right to association, the right to paid holidays, the setting of 
a minimum wage and a maximum number of working hours per week and so on. Each member country 
is invited to ratify these conventions in order to integrate them into its national labour law. 
State regulation and joint negotiations between social partners are therefore necessary in the labour 
market, in order to ensure a fair relationship when negotiating employment contracts and to avoid 
abuse. With these limitations in mind, the supply/demand ratio remains an important market factor. 
This is frequently seen in so-called shortage occupations in many sectors (IT, health, catering and so on), 
in which the scarcity of trained operational people has led to an increase in the level of wages offered 
by employers. 
Labour is therefore not a commodity like any other, but it does react to the laws of the market, which 
must be framed by regulatory limits and parity agreements to avoid abuse. 
The profession of counsellor exists in many professional fields in both the market and non-market 
sectors. Whether working in a bookshop, a funeral parlour, a farm or an employment agency, the 
counsellor always plays the same role. An expert in their field, they greet their client, listen to their 
expressed expectations and ask questions to identify and define their real need, before recommending 
a service or product suited to the individual’s needs. They provide the client with useful information 
and can, if necessary, refer them to other more relevant structures. They are guided in their actions by 
concern for client satisfaction.

While ILO Convention No. 88 commits each country to creating, organizing and providing a Public 
Employment Service, which generally takes the form of a specialized public establishment or a State 
administration, other types of structures are also involved in the field of employment, with teams made 
up of counsellorss :
 X Private employment agencies: these are generally commercial and profit-oriented structures that 
operate to match labour supply and demand, either nationally or internationally. Some also employ 
workers for the purpose of making them available to a third party or user company. ILO Convention 
No. 181 sets out the rules for the operation of these structures. 
 X Socioprofessional support structures : these are private companies or associative structures that 
provide support to people who are generally not very autonomous, in groups or individually, to 
help them find employment. These structures are often specialized in supporting specific groups 
(young people, workers with disabilities, women, migrants and so on) and receive funding from the 
State or private donors to carry out their missions. They may also act as subcontractors to public 
employment services. They support individuals in their search for employment, but also often help 
to resolve social problems blocking their integration. Certain of these structures operate within 
the framework of Insertion par l’Activité Economique (Integration through Economic Activity) 
mechanisms. 
 X Vocational training centres : the mission of vocational training organizations is mainly focused on 
teaching and learning. However, some of them also recruit integration counsellors to prepare their 
trainees for the labour market after graduation.

increasingly offering comprehensive support for individuals, who receive guidance in resolving their social

 X Professional ethics: Employment counsellors must at all times maintain the strictest level of 
confidentiality regarding all aspects of their discussions with jobseekers. They should only obtain 
information that is essential to help the jobseeker make the transition into the labour market and 
this information should remain confidential even after the counselling relationship has ended. No 
third party should have access to this information. The same rules apply to the relationship with 
the employer. Precautions should be taken to ensure that all information entered into computer 
databases is stored securel. 
 X Anti-discrimination : Employment counsellors, especially if they are public officials, must 
participate in the fight against existing discrimination in the labour market and, above all, not 
contribute to it. ILO Convention No. 111, adopted in 1958, states that “the term ‘discrimination’ 
includes.. any distinction, exclusion or preference made on the basis of race, colour, sex, religion, 
political opinion, national extraction or social origin, which has the effect of nullifying or impairing 
equality of opportunity or treatment in employment or occupation”. Since then, other criteria 
have been considered discriminatory: age, sexual orientation, place of residence, state of health, 
disability and so on. Concerning access to employment and the selection of candidates, only the 
candidate’s skills and qualifications should be considered.

Why do some unemployed people not take the step of contacting an employment agency? Three main 
reasons are generally given: 
1. The remoteness and difficulty of access to these agencies.
2. Lack of information about the existence of these agencies and the services that they offer
3. Lack of confidence in the ability of these agencies to provide quality services and effective solutions. 
In contrast, what are the main expectations of those who walk through the door of an employment 
agency? : 
 X To register in the employment service files in order to be identified as a jobseeker and to be able to 
benefit from services and proposals
 X To find job vacancies
 X To receive unemployment benefit, where available 
 X To receive advice from employment experts
 X To access training
 X To access information on the labour market, professions, training courses and so on.
 X First contact with the employment service
Depending on the country and the organization, there are three different ways of making contact: 
 X Via the Internet : the jobseeker has to register on the PES website by filling in an online 
questionnaire and uploading supporting documents, such as identity documents, work certificates 
and so on. After this step, an appointment for a personal interview will be offered, sometimes 
combined with an informative meeting.
 X By telephone : The applicant calls a telephone platform. They have an initial interview with a 
counsellor to carry out an administrative pre-registration. An appointment is made for a personal 
interview, during which they will have to present supporting documents. 
 X Physical reception : The applicant goes directly to an employment agency. They are received by 
a receptionist who identifies their expectations and directs them to the most appropriate contact 
person. They will be registered by a counsellor, either immediately or by appointment. 
On their first visit to an employment agency, the jobseeker may discover a place that is similar to a 
resource centre. Indeed, an employment agency is not just a building in which administrative procedures 
are carried out. It should be a welcoming and user-friendly space providing many services as well as 
information, as shown in the following diagram : 
 X Notice boards for job offers, training offers and competitive offers
 X Free access tools: photocopier, computers to consult websites dedicated to jobseeking, information 
on the labour market, training and so on
 X “Active waiting” areas, enabling people to wait while watching films on professions, consulting 
specialized magazines, and so on
 X Self-documentation spaces.

 X Techniques and stances for conducting interviews
Interviews are the counsellor’s main working tool; it is therefore essential to master the rules and 
techniques. Several authors have written on the subject. We will refer here to the work of the American 
psychologist Carl Rogers, which is very relevant to our field. He has developed a person-centred 
educational approach (9).
According to Rogers, each supported individual must be considered unique in terms of their interests 
and values as a person. To a greater or lesser extent they have conscious resources within them that 
can enable them to react to difficulties and achieve their goals. The role of the counsellor’s support is to 
enable the beneficiary to reflect on their situation in order to access their own resources and initiate a 
dynamic of change. 
To do this, the counsellor must deploy appropriate attitudes, rules and interview techniques : 
 X A positive outlook : respectful and non-judgmental. 
 X An attitude of empathy: making an effort to understand the other person and being receptive to 
their reactions while remaining emotionally independent.
 X Active and benevolent listening that allows the beneficiary to feel understood and encouraged to 
reflect.
 X Semi-directive interviewing, using the answers to come up with new questions that will give 
greater insight.
 X Open-ended questions that encourage expression (as opposed to closed questions that imply a 
yes or no answer)

During the analysis and diagnosis interview, the counsellor was able to offer to set up a personalized 
support programme for the individual. What is it about? 
This support is a “service +” implemented by some PES. Not everyone can afford it, especially in 
a context of mass unemployment. If the counsellor and the jobseeker have defined a tailor-made 
action plan during the first interview, the important thing is to implement this sequence of actions. 
However, some individuals will have difficulty in carrying out these procedures on their own and may 
fall into long-term unemployment. In order to avoid this risk, many PES have been developing this 
new level of service for several years: personalized support. 
The aim is to provide the individual with a contact person who will follow them or her for several 
weeks or months, in the form of regular face-to-face meetings but also remote contacts (telephone, 
video, email and so on) in order to guide and support them through the processes set out in the 
action plan. They will also support them in identifying further processes that will be necessary in 
order for their situation to advance.

X Which public should be supported first? 
In line with ILO Convention No. 88 (already mentioned above), the PES were developed to ensure equal 
access to the “public service”. Their priority, at the time of their creation, was to deploy a network of local 
agencies throughout a country’s national territory, that were capable of providing the same range of 
services to all. For those PES that have achieved this goal, the strategy has subsequently shifted from 
equality (the same service for all) to equity (the best service for everyone). 
EQUALITY EQUITY
The needs of individuals are indeed different and PES must have the capacity to “do more for those who 
need it most”. Personal support will usually be offered to the least independent people. 
In the health sector, autonomy is defined as “a person’s ability to carry out the main activities of daily life 
without assistance, whether physical, mental, social or economic, and to adapt to their environment” (10).
In the field of professional integration, autonomy is generally considered to be a jobseeker’s ability to 
conduct an effective job search without the help of a counsellor.

X Styles of support
The counsellor will offer support to the least autonomous people to guide them through the sequence 
of steps in the action plan and achieve their successful professional integration. But how should this 
support be successfully provided? 
According to Dominique Clavier, an occupational psychologist and clinical psychologist (11), ideally the 
counsellor’s intervention will balance two aspects : 
 X The production axis, which concerns the achievement of objectives by mobilizing tools, methods 
and so on.
 X The relationship axis, which corresponds to the way in which the counsellor manages their 
connections with the individual and involves them in achieving their targeted objectives, with a 
view to personal development. 
UNDERSTANDING AUTONOMY FOR
 PÔLE EMPLOI
Being autonomous in your job search or in implementing your project means not only knowing how to 
take steps alone, but also to know how to make informed decisions and implement effective actions; this 
in turn means:
 Knowing oneself well
 Have a good perception of your situation in relation to your environment
 Set consistent goals
 Know how to mobilize resources wisely to achieve these objectives
To be autonomous is...
 ... unique to each individual
 ... relative: one can be autonomous in one 
or more areas and not in others
 ... dynamic: it is constructed: “to gain 
autonomy”
It is not...
 ... determined according to a category: 
age, disability, level of qualification and so 
on.
 ...absolute: the degree of autonomy is 
different in different areas and contexts
 ...fixed: it is not a definitive state: “we are 
not either autonomous or not autonomous, 
once and for all”

Through the prism of caricature, one could imagine some counsellors, obsessed with the objective of 
integration, deploying “instrumentalist” support: doing things in the place of the individual without 
leaving them any place for reflecting upon and implementing actions. On the other hand, other 
counsellors will focus exclusively on creating a relationship of trust with the individual, promoting 
their well-being and development, but without paying attention to the deadlines for the action plan 
or proposing tools and methods. 
In everyday life, “supporting” means “being with” and “going together towards”. It means guiding, 
supporting and sustaining, while respecting the individual and their choices. It is not a question of 
“doing it for” the persons being supported or obliging them to act in a certain way, but rather of 
giving them support and advice, in a personalized manner when necessary, in constructing and 
managing their pathway. 
The ideal stance is that of the “mediator” counsellor, who provides their support by working on both 
the production aspect and on the beneficiary’s personal development, establishing links between 
the two. They thus reinforce the realism of the project, its roots and its viability, taking into account 
their beneficiary’s internal dynamics as the support is provided.
The aim of the support is not only to solve a specific problem of access to the labour market, it is also 
intended to develop the individual’s autonomy, so that they are more at ease in the environment 
around them and able to manage the other professional transitions that they are likely to face during 
their career.
